title: Day 0 support for Reflection’s Beam on Google Cloud: 5x faster perf with llm-d and NVIDIA Dynamo
raw_text: Today, Reflection released Beam , its first open-weight model built to give developers, researchers, and enterprises open control and customization for frontier software engineering and long-horizon agentic tasks. Released under a permissive Apache 2.0 license with BF16 , FP8 , and NVFP4 checkpoints available at launch, Beam sets a new standard for inference efficiency in the 500B-parameter class by solving complex reasoning and coding problems with 3x to 4x higher reasoning compute efficiency than comparable open models. Alongside today’s release, Google Cloud is announcing day 0 support and ready-to-run deployment recipes for serving Beam on Google Cloud AI Hypercomputer and NVIDIA AI Infrastructure. To help developers get the full benefit of Beam’s token efficiency in production, we worked with Reflection to optimize performance of the underlying serving stack using llm-d (with vLLM) and NVIDIA Dynamo (with SGLang) on Google Cloud: "By deploying our Beam model on Google Cloud, we achieved up to 5x higher performance and 8x lower latency to optimize serving of agentic workloads." - Joe Spisak, VP of Product & Head of Open Source, Reflection With today’s day 0 release on Google Cloud, developers get: Compounding model and system efficiency: Combining Beam’s 3x to 4x reasoning compute efficiency with system-level optimizations on A4X Max instances (NVIDIA GB300 NVL72) for up to 5x higher throughput and 8x lower latency,* and G4 VMs (NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000) for up to 2x higher throughput and 8x lower latency.* High-efficiency multi-turn serving: KV-cache-aware routing, prefill/decode disaggregation, speculative decoding and hierarchical KV cache offloading to Host DRAM and Local SSD reduce redundant prompt recomputation across long coding sessions. Turnkey optimized deployment: Our recommended performance optimized recipes for agentic workloads with llm-d and NVIDIA Dynamo are available in AI-Hypercomputer/gpu-recipes , llm-d repo and Model Garden in Gemini platform with a few clicks. *Based on customer benchmarking Scaling inference requires system-level optimization When evaluating models for agentic coding and tool use, inference efficiency happens at two distinct layers: how efficiently the model reasons and how efficiently the serving system executes multi-turn loops . Model-level efficiency: Reflection’s Beam Reflection designed Beam ( ~501B total parameters with ~23B active parameters per token, and an approximately 1M -token context window) specifically for text-native software engineering and multi-step tool use. It plugs directly into the coding harnesses developers already use, including Reflection’s Mirror CLI, Claude Code, Hermes, OpenCode, and , to resolve GitHub issues, run CLI and DevOps workflows, and complete long-horizon tasks. Because Beam activates only 23B parameters per token and reaches solutions using 3x to 4x fewer reasoning tokens than other comparable open weight models, it dramatically reduces the inference-time compute required for each reasoning step. System-level efficiency: AI Hypercomputer optimized serving Once developers deploy an agent into production, a second set of bottlenecks could appear at the serving layer. In an agentic coding loop, the model is called dozens of times in a single session. With every turn, the coding harness appends new file reads, code diffs, compiler logs, and tool outputs to a shared conversation history that quickly grows to tens or hundreds of thousands of tokens. Even when the model itself generates 3x to 4x fewer reasoning tokens on each turn, the accumulated context window across turns creates two major infrastructure challenges: First, prefill compute becomes a bottleneck . Standard Kubernetes load balancers distribute requests using stateless round-robin routing. When a coding harness sends Turn 15 of a session, it often lands on a different replica than Turn 14. That replica is forced to recompute the entire historical prompt from scratch, wasting GPU compute and creating long prefill queues that delay other users. Second, decode becomes bottlenecked by KV cache capacity . Holding long-context KV caches for dozens of concurrent agent sessions quickly fills up GPU High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM). Once HBM fills up, the serving engine has to evict older KV blocks. As soon as those blocks are evicted, cache hit rates drop and GPU throughput stalls. To preserve Beam’s model-level efficiency at cluster scale, the serving stack has to be optimized as a distributed system. That is why our recipes pair Beam with llm-d (with vLLM) and NVIDIA Dynamo (with SGLang). Inside the AI Hypercomputer inference architecture To run Beam’s BF16 , FP8 , and NVFP4 checkpoints at peak efficiency on Day 0, we designed a vertically integrated architecture on AI Hypercomputer where each layer handles a specific part of the agentic serving lifecycle. System optimized architecture for serving agentic traffic Rather than treating inference pods as stateless endpoints, each layer of the stack is co-designed around the multi-turn agent lifecycle: Prefix- and load-aware routing (GKE + llm-d EPP / Dynamo router): Tracks cached prefixes and queue depth across worker pods, steering each follow-up turn from a coding harness to the replica holding its warm KV prefix while preventing queue saturation via turn-priority flow control. Disaggregated compute and speculative decoding (A4X Max & G4 instance) : Runs vLLM and SGLang with native Blackwell NVFP4, Expert Parallelism (EP) for Beam’s 23B active experts, Data-Parallel Attention, and DFlash2 speculative decoding. Separating Prefill and Decode (P/D) pools ensures heavy prompt bursts never stall active token generation. Tiered KV cache (GPU Memory -> DRAM & Local SSD) Active KV blocks stay in high-bandwidth GPU memory ( Tier 1 ), while warm KV blocks evicted during long-horizon sessions overflow into host CPU DRAM and local NVMe SSDs ( Tier 2 ) via vLLM’s OffloadingConnector or SGLang's HiCache, allowing historical context to be fetched in milliseconds instead of recomputed from scratch. System optimizations for multi-turn agentic workloads When serving multi-turn coding and tool-use workloads like the AgentX trajectory dataset across rising concurrency levels, each layer in the serving stack contributes to the performance and latency improvements for multi-turn, long context traffic patterns of agentic workloads: A note on reading these charts. The two configurations are not comparable to each other. NVIDIA Dynamo ran on A4X Max instances with 32 x NVIDIA GB300 NVL72GPUs; llm-d ran on G4 VMs with 8 x NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs. Each chart shows the gain over a baseline on the same hardware. More replicas give the router more warm KV caches to hit and more room to split prefill from decode, so the uplift grows with the deployment. Both llm-d and NVIDIA Dynamo scale up and down to match the underlying infrastructure. NVIDIA Dynamo optimized perf vs baseline deployment of Reflection's Beam llm-d optimized perf vs baseline deployment of Reflection's Beam Across both platforms, layering these optimizations shifts the Pareto frontier to deliver higher output throughput and faster per-user interactivity simultaneously: Baseline deployment (Stateless round-robin routing). In a standard Kubernetes deployment without prefix awareness, consecutive turns from the same coding session land on different replicas, forcing constant prefill recomputation on historical context and causing throughput to plateau as concurrency scales. KV-cache-aware & flow control routing. Enabling prefix-aware routing in NVIDIA Dynamo or llm-d’s Sticky EPP with turn-priority flow control keeps multi-turn agent trajectories pinned to the replica holding their warm KV cache, immediately cutting Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) latency and freeing up GPU compute, resulting in a significant increase in token throughput. Host DRAM and Local SSD (LSSD) KV offloading. Offloading evicted KV blocks from GPU memory into host DRAM and local NVMe SSDs prevents cache thrashing when dozens of long-context coding sessions exceed on-device GPU memory capacity. Disaggregated serving, speculative decoding, and KV pool tuning. Tuning hybrid KV cache memory allocation, enabling speculative decoding, and disaggregating prefill and decode workers isolates token generation from heavy prompt bursts while the draft model multiplies output throughput to keep per-agent token interactivity fast. All of the Kubernetes manifests, router configurations, and benchmarking scripts from this post are open-source and ready to run on your own GKE cluster. title: Architecting autonomy: A design pattern for high-compute, governed agents in biotech
raw_text: In production systems today, most AI agents operate as lightweight dispatchers. They parse a prompt, make an API call, retrieve a record, and hand back control. Their execution is fast, stateless and cheap. Biotechnology does not work this way. Folding a protein target, screening a 50,000 compound ligand library, or evaluating structure-activity relationships (SAR) are not quick API lookups. They are sustained, stateful, GPU-bound simulations that run for minutes or even hours across specialized silicon. When you ask a general-purpose large language model (LLM) endpoint to coordinate a complex drug discovery workflow, the standard paradigm breaks: Timeouts occur, context windows overflow with atomic coordinates, and proprietary chemical Intellectual Property (IP) risks exposure to external networks. Building enterprise grade research and development (R&D) agents requires moving past the monolithic assistant model. In this blog post, we will discuss how to use a three-layer architecture: separating cognitive orchestration (the brain) from computational execution (the muscle), and anchoring both inside an enterprise governance plane to build scalable agents for drug discovery use cases in biotech. A three-layer pattern The reference architecture below shows how to architect, optimize, and govern high-compute autonomous agents in biotechnology, specifically Drug Discovery. Figure 1 — The three-layer pattern: a cognitive orchestrator (brain), a scalable GPU execution layer (muscle), and an enterprise governance plane. The execution layer: scaling the muscle - high-compute execution The execution layer is responsible for the heavy scientific computations. The first architectural decision is determining where workloads should run: Strategic, proprietary pipelines require dedicated GPU infrastructure within your security perimeter Routine or standardized workloads can safely be delegated to managed cloud endpoints In this architecture, protein folding is driven by ESMFold and generative design by GenMol . Both run as NVIDIA Inference Microservices or NIMs deployed on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) using G4 VMs backed by NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs. A critical hurdle in containerized GPU workloads is the cold-start penalty, the latency delay required to pull multi-gigabyte model weights from an image registry and stage them into GPU memory (VRAM). To ensure low latency responsiveness, we build the following as a recommendation into the reference architecture: Maintain warm pools: Pin the GKE node pool to a minimum of one active node. Preload weights: Model weights are loaded directly into VRAM at pod initialization, ensuring containers are immediately ready for inference. Resilient scheduling: GKE manages pod lifecycles and restarts failed instances without tearing down the underlying VM infrastructure. This approach trades custom, manual CUDA kernel tuning for NVIDIA's pre-compiled, containerized runtimes, dramatically reducing infrastructure engineering overhead while ensuring deterministic throughput. In biotech, chemical structures represent millions of dollars in proprietary IP. A docking request transmits SMILE strings or 3D coordinate matrices that must never leave company custody. Containerized NIMs eliminate the friction between rapid prototyping and rigorous data isolation. During early exploration, researchers can query NVIDIA hosted endpoints. When transitioning to proprietary lead candidates, the exact same container is deployed to GKE inside a private VPC . The agent’s orchestration logic remains identical; only the target URI updates from an external proxy to an internal VPC endpoint. No structural data leaves the enterprise perimeter. The cognitive layer: Multi-agent reasoning With compute execution isolated, the cognitive layer manages agentic workflow sequencing. Built on Agent Runtime , within the Gemini platform, this reference architecture shows a system that deploys a hierarchical multi-agent structure, one lead orchestrator, and two specialized domain sub-agents (Lead Optimization and Safety Screening) . The multi-agent design can be modified to suit the use case at hand. Based on this design, when an end-user submits a high-level task such as “ Analyze Candidate 4b against Target X and produce a SAR report” , the system applies four core orchestration patterns discussed below; In-process native agent handoffs: The lead orchestrator delegates tasks to specialist sub-agents using Agent Runtime’s native SDK rather than network-serialized agent-to-agent HTTP protocols. This eliminates intermediate network hops and keeps internal handoffs instantaneous. Only the outermost boundary communicates outward to user-facing surfaces like the Gemini agent. Passing bulky payloads by reference: LLMs degrade quickly when forced to ingest massive arrays of 3D spatial coordinates. In this architecture, raw structural data (PDB files, docking poses, trajectory logs) is written directly to Cloud Storage . Agents pass lightweight, signed object URIs and high-level structural summaries, keeping context windows compact and inference costs down. Decoupling workflow logic from biochemical reasoning: General-purpose LLMs excel at task planning and synthesis, but are prone to hallucinating biochemical nuances. To control this behavior, this architecture maintains strong separation of concerns, namely, workflow and tasks decomposition are handled by Gemini. Domain chemistry and pharmacological reasoning are handled by specialized Nemotron models hosted on dedicated GPU nodes. Context-driven evaluation over rigid cutoffs: Traditional computational screening enforces arbitrary numerical cutoffs (e.g., discard if binding affinity ,-7.5 kcal/mol) However, therapeutic context fundamentally alters risk tolerance. Preventive cardiovascular therapy taken daily by healthy patients requires extremely strict safety margins, or a novel oncology candidate targeting an intractable cancer may accept higher toxicity if efficacy is demonstrated. By passing disease context directly into the specialized reasoning models, drug candidates are evaluated against dynamic, target-specific profiles rather than static thresholds, preventing the premature culling of viable drug leads. Performance best practices for high-compute pipelines Optimizing an agentic system that interfaces with heavy GPU compute requires challenging common engineering instincts: Common Assumption Architectural Reality Recommended Best Practice "Swap in a faster driver model to cut latency." The primary orchestrator's token generation is rarely the bottleneck in multi-step R&D pipelines. Optimize I/O, not token speed: Focus on reducing payload sizes and intermediate network hops rather than compromising orchestrator reasoning depth. "Parallelize tool calls across workers." External scientific services and containerized models often serialize requests internally on dedicated hardware. Respect execution topology: Align client-side concurrency with backend queue mechanics to prevent pipeline lockouts and connection timeouts. "Pass full simulation states between tools." Large JSON bodies cause schema validation failures, prompt truncation, and token bloat. Pass heavy payloads by reference: Store raw coordinates in object storage and pass lightweight URIs between agent boundaries. "Return outputs only when the pipeline finishes." Long multi-minute runs leave scientists blind to whether jobs are proceeding or stalled. Stream intermediate stage completions: Emit progress updates at each completed milestone (e.g., folding complete , docking running ) for real-time visibility. "Chain multiple granular micro-tools." Deep tool-chains increase the probability of hallucinated arguments and schema mismatches. Collapse compute pipelines: Wrap end-to-end simulation pipelines behind a single, clean tool interface that takes clear parameters and returns a consolidated object. The enterprise governance and asymmetric autonomy Deploying high-compute agents in enterprise environments requires robust data sovereignty, audit trails, and process control. The Gemini platform establishes these safeguards natively with the following components: Agent Identity : Every autonomous agent operates with a cryptographically verifiable identity. Thus, for a biotech use case, when a candidate molecule is advanced or rejected, the event is permanently logged to that specific agent principal. Agent Gateway : This serves the single ingress/egress point for every interaction within the perimeter. Centralized IAM and regional residency rules help ensure sensitive molecular data remains within designated cloud regions. Agent Registry : This feature maintains a curated catalog of approved agents, validated tool schemas, and authorized Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, preventing rogue tools from executing in production. Model Armor : This functionality inspects incoming prompts and outgoing payloads in real time to prevent prompt injection and data exfiltration. The payoff is clear. Identity, RBAC, auditing, residency, and data protection are native properties of the Gemini platform; this allows enterprise customers to focus on science rather than having to build a compliance stack for every project. In high-stakes research and development, full autonomy introduces unacceptable liability, while requiring approval for trivial steps can create frictions. The solution addressing this to use asymmetric gating in the following ways; Automate reversible operations: For example, allow the agent to resolve chemical naming synonyms, pull structural PDBs, and run preliminary Lipinski screens autonomously without interrupting the researcher. Gate irreversible operations: For instance, initiating multi-GPU docking run, advancing a lead compound to wet-lab synthesis, or archiving a therapeutic program must require explicit human sign-off. The pattern, and the path forward High-compute autonomous agents succeed when the boundaries between cognitive planning, numerical computation, and system governance are clean in the following ways: Keep the orchestrator focused on decomposition and synthesis, leaving intensive biophysical simulation to specialized, containerized microservices and models. Eliminate context bloat by passing complex chemical data by reference through cloud storage. Anchor the workflow in enterprise governance, pairing cryptographic agent identity with asymmetric human oversight. As generative and structural biology models expand toward whole-cell modeling and complex dynamic simulations, this decoupled architecture ensures research systems scale efficiently while keeping proprietary IP secure and auditable. summary: In production systems today, most AI agents operate as lightweight dispatchers. They parse a prompt, make an API call, retrieve a record, and hand back control. Their execution is fast, stateless and cheap. Biotechnology does not work this way.

Performance and operational overhead : Without explicit and strategic resource limits, runtime agents can impact how much CPU and memory is available for your workloads and system functionality. title: Four evaluation engineering lessons learned from building agent plugins
raw_text: The real challenge of building an agentic system isn't the construction, it's the measurement. Evaluation engineering is a critical foundation for building reliable AI systems. Setting up systematic, repeatable tests to measure your agent’s true behavior can be the difference between shipping a tool you can trust and one that silently breaks, fails to call APIs, or makes mistakes. I’ve run evaluation engineering initiatives for years at Google and d eveloping the newly released Google Cloud Developer plugin served as a live testbed to stress-test these key principles across real-world developer workflows. Here are four eval lessons we learned from building the new plugin that you can apply to your own builds. 1. Grade the execution steps instead of the summary When we first evaluated agents, we set up an LLM-as-judge to inspect the agent’s final text reply and scored it against a checklist. However, we quickly realized it’s fundamentally flawed because the grader only sees what the agent wrote, not what it actually did. When we ran our initial 11-prompt evaluation suite for the Google Cloud Developer plugin, the automated grader marked it as failing three prompts. But when we opened the raw tool-call logs and read the transcripts, the plugin had actually passed all three. On a Cloud Run cleanup prompt, for instance, our rubric required checking command syntax before running anything. The agent ran gcloud help run services list as its very first step. It did the work, but its final message was focused on warning the user about permanent data loss rather than reciting that it had checked the help docs. The grader penalized the agent for doing the right thing simply because it didn’t brag about it in the summary. If your rubric line says "did it run X?", a LLM judge is guessing unless you evaluate the actual tool-call trajectory. Takeaway : Don't grade an agent on its closing pitch. Score the raw execution trajectory to verify what commands were actually executed, validated, and scoped. 2. Design evals for asynchronous operations When you start reading tool-call trajectories, how you extract that telemetry matters just as much as what you're reading. Extracting agent telemetry into a flattened, sequential list of events obscures concurrent tool dispatch, which is one of the critical causes of behavioral failure. Modern agent harnesses often batch multiple tool invocations into a single assistant turn using an array of calls. In our evaluations, when an agent was asked to inspect an environment and look up documentation, the harness dispatched the skill-loading call and two documentation searches simultaneously within a single tool_calls payload. Because activating a skill is a multi-stage process, where the initial call returns a short launch stub and the subsequent turn injects the full instruction body, the instructions meant to govern the search arrived in the prompt context after the system had already executed the searches. The system never gave the skill a dedicated turn to let its guidance influence the agent's actions. If telemetry pipelines strip out turn structures and merge calls into a flat timeline, engineers will waste days wondering why an agent disregarded unambiguous instructions that a developer embedded in a skill. Takeaway : Preserve turn structure in telemetry extractors so you can identify when client-side parallel dispatch issues tool calls before injected guidance enters the context window. 3. Test live runs and "dry runs" side-by-side You need to inspect real API calls to catch harness quirks, like parallel dispatch. But if you only test your agent in one environment condition, you're flying half-blind. From day one, you need to run two conditions side-by-side: a live run and a plan-only run. In the live condition, the agent has real, sandboxed credentials and actually executes commands. This is how you see if syntax works, parameters serialize cleanly, and the agent exercises restraint before doing something destructive. Live runs frequently hit an unexpected permission error on step two and abort before you ever reach the behavior you’re trying to test. That's why you need the plan-only condition, where you strip credentials and tell the agent to explain what it would do without running anything. This strips out permission roadblocks and shows you the model’s pure reasoning and routing intent. Roughly half our most important findings came from the delta between the two. For example, on one of our onboarding prompts, a live run was blocked immediately on a project list call. The plan-only run sailed right through and produced an 8,000-character plan that completely ignored organization policies, admin approvals, and governance. The live run masked a major cognitive flaw that the plan-only run exposed in seconds. Takeaway : Run live and plan-only evaluations side by side. Live runs test actual execution and safety restraint; plan-only runs expose the model's raw reasoning and routing without getting tripped up by permission errors. 4. Use “golden sets” as durable baselines Frontier model architectures change every few months, agent harnesses improve, and plugin manifest standards will inevitably evolve. When building the Google Cloud Developer plugin, we treated evaluations as continuous integration testing for these non-deterministic environments. That means we stress-tested the composite stack, including the harness, the live model, and the tools running together on realistic tasks. Instead of guessing from the final text output, this approach captures the whole trajectory: what the agent thought, what commands it actually ran, and whether it solved the problem without breaking anything. Then you score that run against golden sets curated by real human experts who know what the ideal path looks like. Takeaway : Build golden sets based on what the entire system should actually do in the wild, including your harness, model, and plugins. Models change, but those baseline runs are your safety net. Reminder: Use evaluation suites over “one-shot” demos A common mistake I see among engineers is what I like to call the one-shot demo. This is when someone feeds a prompt into a LLM, watches it build a complete 3D game or solves a Rubik’s cube in a single pass and calls it an eval. But in reality, this is just a vanity metric. To do quality work with AI, I truly believe that you need evaluation suites. Without evaluations, teams are like literally running into a dark cave blind. Engineering an enterprise-grade agent means testing the system's ability to handle multi-step interactions, manage permissions, and avoid destructive outcomes like accidentally deleting a project because you asked it to "find opportunities to save costs." Where to go from here Building an agent plugin or MCP server is the beginning. Shipping something you can actually trust with real cloud infrastructure requires significantly more work in evaluations to ensure it’s doing what you expect it to do. At the end of the day, the only thing that outlasts model churn is a stress-tested eval suite. Check out the Google Cloud Developer plugin documentation or explore this codelab to get started with the plugin in Antigravity.

title: The SAVE method: Learn the fundamentals to engineer trustworthy generative media
raw_text: Google Cloud Consulting works with organizations every day to build generative media that’s trustworthy, brand-aligned, and stands out. Instead of relying on clever or complicated prompting, we’ve identified four recurring basics to generate consistent results, what we call the “SAVE” method. In this blog, we’ll share more about this method and how you can apply it to your own work. S - Separate the researcher from the storyteller If in a single prompt, if you’re requesting a technical summary, key product features, and an engaging video script all at once, you’re setting the model up to fail. Creative tasks require fluid language and pacing, while factual output requires constraint. Forcing both jobs into one context window will likely end with the model fabricating details to make the narrative flow better. Instead of one prompt, consider splitting the work into specialized steps, like a researcher and a storyteller. Here’s how they might work together: The researcher reads the source documents, extracts core claims, aligns with approved messaging, and outputs a structured brief (like a clean checklist or bulleted factsheet). The storyteller then takes that verified brief and focuses purely on style, pacing, visual metaphors, and tone. By decoupling research from your creative generation, your agent is never tasked with deciding what’s true, but how to make the truth more engaging and effective. A - Approve verified facts only If you hand a creative generative model documents that are unedited, it might mix up speculative ideas with business facts. The media generator should never have direct access to raw source files. It should only use verified, structured inputs. To avoid this: Lock down core claims : Approved statements, product names, and concrete business outcomes should be fixed upstream rather than left for the model to extract on the spot. Champion contextual packaging : Pass each fact along with its explicit constraints included. Examples may include things like "use this point in the opening statement" or "do not extrapolate beyond this approved bullet point." This way, you ground the generation in verified facts and reduce the risk of unsupported claims entering the creative generation stage. V - Verify before you render Discovering a factual error in an animated video or rendered asset after the final export wastes both compute budget and turnaround time. The most effective human-in-the-loop checkpoint is right before generation begins. To fix this, review the script and storyboard. Have product leads or legal teams sign off on the extracted facts, narrative outline, and voiceover text while it’s still simple, editable text. This way, you can catch errors early. Swapping an outdated feature name or fixing a typo takes two seconds in a text file. Treat text as your testing ground. Once approved, generating the final media becomes a low-risk, predictable step. E - Engineer guardrails into the system Telling a model to “keep voiceover word count short, never reference unapproved topics, and format links correctly" in a prompt works until it doesn’t, and an edge case slips through. Relying on prompt obedience for brand safety is a gamble and can damage trust. Where requirements can be checked deterministically, enforce them in the system rather than relying only on prompt instructions. For example, try these three actions first: Programmatic boundary checks : Use standard code to validate word counts, verify that URLs are live and authorized, check colors against your brand palette, and format text strings. Independent safety gates : Run automated filters outside the generation pipeline to catch policy violations or out-of-bounds claims before an asset is ever delivered. Model modularity : When your safety and brand rules are set, you don't have to rewrite your entire governance playbook every time a newer, faster generative model is launched. You simply plug the new model into your existing, verified pipeline. Generating studio-quality media shouldn't mean constantly worrying about what the model might fabricate next. The SAVE method shifts the burden of accuracy away from prompt phrasing and into the architecture where it belongs. title: Hallucinated domain in official OpenAI skill underscores AI supply chain risks
raw_text: Researchers have discovered a first-of-its-kind supply-chain vulnerability in OpenAI’s official skills repository. OpenAI maintains an official GitHub repository of skills that teach AI agents how to work with various platforms and services. As an official skill, these components are often given an implicit level of trust because they are contributed or vetted by verified vendors. Snags arose because one OpenAI skill — designed to teach agents the best way to deploy applications on Render — instructed production apps to send their tokens to an unregistered domain ( render-internal.com ). Discovering this flaw, researchers from AIR Security’s Research Lab registered the domain and pointed it at a passive (listening-only) sinkhole, which started receiving tokens and API calls from real production apps. Testing the skill with Codex confirmed that the domain made its way into real application code as the default option. AIR Security informed OpenAI and Render of the issue, which was resolved in mid-August, allowing its researchers to publish a technical write-up of the flaw . The issue was introduced with a commit in January. Render removed every render-internal.com reference from the skill while OpenAI purged the Render plugin from openai/plugins. The domain was also transferred to Render’s safe holding. The curated skill contained a hallucinated domain that deployed applications treated as a trusted internal service, putting their secrets within reach of whoever registered it. Supply chain risk If researchers hadn’t stumbled across Render skill flaw first, attackers might have abused a domain nobody bothered to buy to run a supply chain attack. Niv Hoffman, AIR Security’s co-founder and CTO, said the incident shows that even official, vendor-published AI skills can contain mistakes, unsafe assumptions, dependencies, or vulnerabilities that can lead to exfiltration of secret tokens. “Skills should be vetted and monitored like any other part of the software supply chain, so they can be patched or revoked when a vulnerability is found in one of them,” Hoffman said. Attackers are increasingly exploring new ways of manipulating AI instruction files such as skills toward malicious ends, while also seeking AI credentials to steal or misuse to operationalize their own use of AI . A recent Trojanized AI skill that typosquatted popular AI-related services Paperclip and Browser Use on open agent skills ecosystem skills.sh garnered 1.7M installations in a scheme to instruct agents to install a credential stealer from GitHub instead.

title: Xbow spent $40K on AI and cracked Google Chrome wide open
raw_text: A chain of vulnerabilities in Google’s Chrome browser could have enabled researchers to take control of one billion Windows machines worldwide — and it cost them just $40,000 in AI compute time to discover it. Researchers at Xbow USA worked for six days on developing the exploit , which earned them a $250,000 bug bounty from Google, the first under the new 2026 rules . They chose OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol for the task to demonstrate what’s possible with a publicly available model rather than a specialist security implementation. They used it to search Chrome’s source code, test ideas, and build proofs of concept, while they set the strategy, chose where to look, and checked its work. They successfully chained together a vulnerability to escape first from the sandbox containing the V8 JavaScript engine and then from Chrome’s operating-system process sandbox, launching a Windows app from within a malicious web page. Xbow presented its findings to Google, which fixed the flaws. The researchers set out all the details as to how the exploit was developed in a blog . This article first appeared on Computerworld .

title: Linux kernel gets a fix for a flaw that enabled attackers to escape VMs
raw_text: The Linux kernel’s networking stack was found vulnerable to a guest-to-host escape attack , in which an attacker operating inside a virtual machine (VM) could cross the isolation boundary and access the underlying host. Dubbed PwnEscape and tracked as CVE-2026-99999, a flaw allowed guest-controlled packet metadata to trigger a write that changes an IPv4 header after the kernel has already processed it. That flaw could be chained with additional exploitation techniques to achieve host-level code execution. The problem was discovered by security researcher Paulos Yibelo of Pwn.ai while participating in Vercel’s $1 million Sandbox security challenge, announced on August 18. The challenge invited researchers to test the isolation boundaries of Vercel’s sandboxing infrastructure, including whether they could escape the virtual machine itself and reach the host. Vercel subsequently described PwnEscape as the most severe finding submitted through its program. “The packet-related crash and code execution attacks were demonstrated on the researcher’s own KVM and Firecracker machines matching Vercel Sandbox configuration,” Vercel’s principal security engineer Andy Riancho said in a blog post . No reports showed anyone accessing customer data in Vercel Sandbox, he added. The issue is now resolved. An NVD description of the bug identified seven stable-branch fixes, including Linux versions 5.10 , 5.15 , 6.1 , 6.6 , 6.12 , 6.18 , and 7.2 , and one mainline fix . Delayed checksum changed kernel-trusted header PwnEscape exploits Linux’s checksum-offloading mechanism, which allows the kernel to defer calculating a network packet’s checksum until a later stage of processing. The packet’s metadata specifies where the calculation should begin and where its result should be written. The problem arises when attacker-controlled checksum metadata directs that write into the packet’s IPv4 header. Linux initially processes the packet using its original header, but a later checksum-completion operation can change the header before fragmentation code consumes it again. Yibelo demonstrated this by successfully changing the IPv4 header’s interpreted length from 20 bytes to 60 bytes. The fragmented code then treated bytes beyond the packet’s valid data as part of the header, allowing 32 bytes of adjacent host memory to be included in an outgoing packet. This is effectively a time-of-check/time-of-use ( TOCTOU ) problem: the kernel makes security-relevant decisions using one version of the header, then later acts on a modified version without revalidating it. However, the sequence does not require the usual race between threads; the deferred write occurs during normal networking operations, Yibelo said in a blog post. Linux’s fix guards the checksum write The accepted upstream fix, commit 6785011f8b16, introduces validation checks before the relevant checksum-completion operations. These checks prevent the checksum write from corrupting the IPv4 header along the affected processing paths. The patch was applied to the Linux development tree on October 8 and merged into the mainline kernel on October 14, according to the blog post. Yibelo described the change as a defence-in-depth measure, noting that broader validation of untrusted checksum metadata remains an area for further work. Yibelo reported chaining the memory leak with additional exploitation steps to achieve selected kernel-memory writes and execute a host-root helper on its own test systems. “We used the resulting capability in a bounded lab chain to execute a host-root helper and return a host-generated marker to the guest. Four separate true-cold boots completed that chain,” he said. While further details of how Yibelo achieved the guest-to-host escape are awaited, he stressed that the issue is not specific to KVM or another hypervisor, but lies in the Linux networking stack that handles guest traffic. “Although we suspect the security industry will use this post to figure out the other affected hypervisors and we expect exploits in weaker configurations to arrive in weeks, and exploits working in default hypervisor configurations to arrive in under a month,” Yibelo warned.

title: BeyondTrust zero-day tied to Chinese spies puts Remote Support users on alert
raw_text: Organizations running self-hosted BeyondTrust Remote Support should treat exposed appliances as potentially compromised after a suspected Chinese espionage group exploited a critical zero-day to gain root control, access credential vaults, and establish footholds for lateral movement, according to Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group. “Organizations should prepare for potential widespread exploitation following this disclosure,” Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant said in a blog post. The post attributes the zero-day exploitation to ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor formerly tracked as UNC5221, and dates it to late August. BeyondTrust disclosed the flaw, CVE-2026-102764 , the same day in advisory BT26-05 and said it had already released a patch on Oct. 8. According to the CVE record, it scores 9.3 on CVSS 4.0 and affects Remote Support versions up to 26.2.3. Mandiant said an unauthenticated attacker can exploit it to perform file operations, leading to host-level control and access to every credential the appliance stores or brokers. BeyondTrust urged self-hosted customers to apply the patch immediately and said in a blog post that it is withholding technical details while they do. A month undetected BeyondTrust’s timeline puts the first exploitation on Aug. 29, against one BeyondTrust-hosted instance and one self-hosted appliance. The company found the intrusion on Sept. 28, after another vendor’s edge appliances were publicly reported as compromised and Mandiant sent a brief, non-specific warning. “Our sensors fired in real time when the actor escalated privileges,” BeyondTrust wrote in the blog. The built-in triage tool in its third-party detection platform then closed those alerts as false positives, the company said, without naming the vendor. BeyondTrust said it contained the hosted instance 27 minutes after identifying it and is working with the vendor, so automated triage cannot close high-severity signals on its own. Neither company has said whether other customers were compromised. Root, persistence, and log wiping About 11 minutes after the first malicious request, a PHP web shell Mandiant calls SAWFLY appeared in the appliance’s web root, Google said in the blog post. To escalate from SAWFLY’s unprivileged service account, the actor copied /bin/sh to /usr/bin/dbus-authd, made root its owner, and set the SUID bit, Mandiant said. It then planted a startup script that writes a passwordless sudo entry into BeyondTrust’s sudoers template, so the access survives reboots and configuration resets. It later deleted more than a dozen system, web server, and application logs. Turning the help desk tool against its owner In the blog post Mandiant added that the attacker raised the account’s Jump Item and Team permissions from No Access to Administrator using a compromised administrator account. “This configuration change granted the threat actor permanent, unrestricted authorization to launch remote sessions to downstream systems populated within the appliance’s Jump Item list,” the blog post added. It also deployed BARECLAW, a custom SOCKS5 tunneler, and edited the appliance’s HAProxy configuration to route traffic to it through a hidden local listener, the post noted. Older versions must first be upgraded, and upgrading does not remediate prior exposure. It advises rotating credentials only after patching, so new secrets do not land on a box the attacker still controls. BeyondTrust said CrowdStrike tracks the same cluster as WARP PANDA. “It is possible that we will observe similar widespread exploitation attempts associated with CVE-2026-102764,” Mandiant said in the post. GTIG compared the risk to 2024, when the group moved to mass exploitation after Ivanti Connect Secure flaws were disclosed. In 2025, it turned an Ivanti patch into a working exploit. BeyondTrust said it suspects, without forensic proof, that the actor uses AI to model the products it targets, echoing a GTIG finding that attackers are weaponizing newly disclosed flaws faster. BT26-05 is BeyondTrust’s third critical-rated Remote Support advisory this year, according to its advisory index. title: Cyberattack AIs must be trained only on air-gapped systems, hundreds of AI researchers say
raw_text: Current security procedures for training AI models are inadequate, hundreds of AI researchers have warned governments and the AI community. They are calling for tougher rules and the establishment of a new international body overseeing best practice for AI development. In an open letter the AI specialists — 487, at time of publication, including many senior academics — called for more AI safety research and greater emphasis on containment technologies. “Strong sandboxing mechanisms including air-gapping (disconnecting from the internet) should be used to provide high-assurance containment of cyber-capable AI models,” say the signatories, who include such luminaries as Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio. The experts said that a new international body, to be set up in consultation with governments and a wide range of AI and security specialists, could set new safety standards but also act as an organization to which containment failures could be reported, improving transparency for learning and accountability purposes. The scientists’ demands go further than some recent calls for greater regulation of AI. Earlier this week, Microsoft president Brad Smith said AI is less regulated than washing machines or milk, although he made no firm proposals to rectify the situation. And the UK parliament is looking at ways to improve AI security , although any moves will be hampered by disagreement among AI businesses. Hinton and Bengio are no strangers to this kind of scientist-led initiative. In October last year, they signed an open letter warning of the dangers of developing super-intelligent AI . The letter appears not to have affected AI’s breakneck development; it remains to be seen whether AI players in boardrooms will heed the warning.

title: Malware evasion made easier with AI — but behavior still gives it away
raw_text: Fresh research suggests recent panic over AI-generated malware may be overblown. Last month Anthropic detailed how Russia-linked cyberespionage group Midnight Blizzard used Claude to rebuild malware each time security tools flagged its backdoor as malign. “We observed GTG-20006 operate through customized AI-driven workflows that automated much of their operations from development, infrastructure acquisition, phishing, persistence through command and control, to data exfiltration,” the AI company wrote in its report, referring to Midnight Blizzard, aka APT29 and Cozy Bear, as GTG-20006. While the group’s use of AI as part of its operations is notable, what raised eyebrows was how it did so as part of its evasion strategy: “If their monitoring AI agents identified that any of their deployed malware was detected by a security product, agents would then set about the process of autonomously modifying and rebuilding the malware to evade the existing detections. The agents were designed to continue iterating on GTG-20006’s toolkit until it was undetected,” Anthropic reported. That autonomous loop — from monitoring for detection to rebuilding the malware to fine-tune evasion — raises the spectre of polymorphic AI malware , malicious software that changes its code structure automatically while keeping the same core functionality. But threat intelligence company ReversingLabs (RL) has since released a report detailing how its telemetry and behavior-based threat hunting flagged the campaign’s Go backdoor PowerShell stager as malicious on Aug. 1, weeks before Anthropic’s Sept. 10 report. RL subsequently saw five versions of the same stager over the course of 25 days. Although each had a different hash, all five behaved the same way. That consistent behavior profile left each iteration open to detection, according to a technical blog post by ReversingLabs published last week, as analysts could still hunt for what the malware did and how its files and infrastructure were connected. As a result, evasion via AI rebuilds may not yet be as foolproof as first feared. Variations on a well-worn theme Changing a file to dodge detection is one of the oldest techniques in the business, and polymorphic malware has been deployed to dodge signatures for decades. “What stands out with this Midnight Blizzard activity is outsourcing the busywork to an LLM,” says Ben Bernstein, manager of the cybersecurity advisors team at managed detection and response firm Huntress. “They wired an AI agent to monitor security tools and automatically generate fresh variants without human intervention. We have seen basic script automation do this, but large language models just make the refactoring cleaner and faster.” Huntress backs ReversingLabs’ argument that while AI makes malware faster to rebuild it fails to change the hallmarks of its malicious behavior. “Models are fantastic at scrambling code structure and swapping variables to bypass static analysis,” says Bernstein. “But the AI is not inventing novel exploits. It just automates the grunt work of rewriting the same script to ensure the file hashes change.” In short, Bernstein says, “the packaging looks different, but the payload’s core objective remains exactly the same.” Malicious experiments in AI-assisted malware development Still, AI-assisted malware rebuilding is an emerging if not unprecedented tactic among malware developers. For example, Google documented PromptFlux in late 2025 , an experimental script that asked Gemini to rewrite its own source every hour, and PromptSteal, which APT28 used against Ukraine to generate commands at runtime. In March 2026, Microsoft released a report describing how the North Korean cluster Coral Sleet is using agentic AI tools to generate, test, and deploy payloads. “Most of these are early or experimental, and Microsoft’s own assessment is that the capability ‘remain[s] limited by reliability, latency, and operational risk,’” says Igor Lasic, SVP of engineering at ReversingLabs. But this most recent case involving Midnight Blizzard is the “clearest one on record,” according to Lasic, because two independent sources described the same infrastructure: Microsoft on July 31 as CaptiveCrunch , naming the files CornFlake and ChocoShell, and Anthropic on Sept. 10 with visibility into how the operator used Claude. “We held both files from July 6 and July 10, before either report,” says Lasic. Persistent limitations Still, ReversingLabs’ recent report may reflect only the current state of the art of AI-assisted malware rebuilding, as some of the limitations that characterized the Midnight Blizzard instance could be something more advanced models might overcome, Lasic concedes. “Today a model rewrites the file for free but cannot cheaply rewrite the server code that parses the beacon, re-register domains or re-phish victims, so the indicators that survived were the ones that had to change in two places at once,” Lasic explains. “A more capable agent with access to the whole operation could coordinate those changes, and I expect infrastructure indicators to age faster over the next few years, the way hashes already have.” While cost and the availability of more sophisticated models is perhaps only a temporary limit for AI-assisted malware rebuilding, two other limits are closer to fundamental: the behavior of malicious code and clues left behind during a malicious campaign that enable detection. “An implant that steals credentials has to read the credential store and one that calls home has to open a connection, whatever built it,” says Lasic. “Obfuscation makes that harder to extract, but no rewrite removes a requirement without removing the capability.” Furthermore, a model can change the next build but not the builds already observed, timestamped and linked to the same server. “Rebuilding faster produces more artefacts, and each one is another thread back to the operation,” Lasic concludes. Huntress’ Bernstein backs ReversingLabs assessment that behavior-based hunting will remain effective against even AI-assisted malware development. “You can disguise malicious code all day, but if a script tries to dump credentials or establish persistence, most modern EDRs [endpoint detection and response tools] will detect the action itself,” says Bernstein. Another limitation of AI-assisted malware development is that even the latest models are trained to abuse known security vulnerabilities. “They [AI models] remix known patterns rather than dreaming up zero-days,” Bernstein concludes. “Future models might get better if they can actively test their output against live environments to find undiscovered flaws, but for now, they are just recycling known techniques at a higher speed.”

title: FPT and its ilk offer an alternative to Indian offshorers
raw_text:
When it was announced that Wipro would exit India’s wonderfully named “Nifty 50” index of powerhouse stocks at the end of September 2026, it felt if not quite the end of an era, then a tapering off of what was once an uber-trend in the modern IT services sector.

Indian IT offshorers boomed through the enterprise resource planning (ERP) charge of the late 1990s as enterprises sought to protect against the looming fallout of the Y2K bug and join up what had been mismatched enterprise applications.

Bloomberg saw the Wipro episode as reflecting the “waning clout” of Indian giants, and it may be the case that India has been challenged by an increasingly saturated market. But the news may also have been reflective of a more slow-burning trend: the rise of other services firms worldwide with the skills, hunger and culture to address artificial intelligence (AI) and other emerging opportunities with a strong value proposition. 

Keen viewers of World Cup football pitchside banners may have noted the presence of Argentina’s Globant, while there are also significant players operating globally with roots in Malaysia, China and the Philippines.

But perhaps the most interesting of the insurgents is FPT, the Vietnamese juggernaut that is carving more than a niche through outsourcing, software development and other adjacent opportunities in much the same way that the likes of Wipro, Tata, Infosys and others from India did all those years ago.

Star of Asia

Vietnam is the star turn of southeast Asia’s growth, growing at over 8%, faster even than fast-risers such as Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia. The country is consistently ranked as the top regional outperformer by McKinsey. Growth in the region is powered by technology, with Vietnam aspiring to become a global top 25 economy by 2038, propelled by state-backed initiatives to weave a digital identity, banking and government services fabric, supported by ubiquitous mobile broadband.

The virtuous circle also includes robust foreign financial investment, helping to attract the likes of tech superpowers including Apple, Intel, Nvidia and Samsung. A healthy portion of those investments focus on research and development (R&D) and sophisticated low-level engineering activities such as semiconductor fabrication.

But the jewel in the crown of Vietnamese tech scene is indisputably FPT, a wide-ranging player in software development, outsourcing, digital transformation, telecoms and infrastructure. The company even has its own university campuses where legions of the country’s youth pursue digital dreams and from whom FPT can cherry-pick talent.

FPT has become increasingly hard to miss. Its logo has even been on the sleeves of Chelsea FC footballers, the London club with which it has an ongoing partnership for fan experience and other transformation projects. And outside the rarefied world of elite sport, FPT is making inroads in both the public and private sectors of the UK and other countries outside its homeland.

Dang Tran Phuong, FPT head of Europe and Middle East, who joined FPT in 2004 and has held management roles in FPT’s US market unit and across key accounts in aviation and logistics, said its ambitions are sky-high, and its plan is to replicate its formula from its native country. 

“We believe that the UK and other countries want similar things,” he said. “Value, time to market and new skills. We are an AI-first company and we are good at complex challenges that can serve the UK, such as quantum computing and building AI skills.”

“We are an AI-first company and we are good at complex challenges that can serve the UK, such as quantum computing and building AI skills.”

Dang Tran Phuong, FPT

By focusing on AI and other emerging technologies, Phuong believes FPT has the formula to succeed everywhere. The firm’s current strategy encompasses nearshoring opportunities that capitalise on Vietnam’s choice geographical location, but also extends to having a global reach.

Phuong noted that FPT now has 85,000 staff across 30 countries, and 1,100 customers. Overseas outsourcing deals are up about 30% year on year (YoY) and $10m-plus outsourcing contracts are becoming more common. FPT recorded almost $2.7bn in total revenue in 2025. 

AI, of course

Emblematic of the rapid change and pursuit of a market-altering inflexion point is AI, seen by FPT and Phuong as a way to fast-track its progress in a world seeking talent in the space. However, he added, software engineering, industrial transformation, computer visualisation and even drones are on its menu of offers.

More recently, FPT has extended its ecosystem and the company now has far-reaching connections to many of the core technology providers that are critical to Western ambitions, such as Salesforce, Palantir, AWS, OpenAI and Sitecore. 

Another key area is cyber security, where FPT recently inked a deal with OpenAI to proactively protect customers using AI frontier models and agentic adaptations to processes and workflows. Rather than using third-party alternatives, FPT uses Casan, its own five-stage transformation maturity framework that lets clients evolve from ‘curious’ to a sophisticated ‘native’ stage, via augmented, standard and automatic steps. 

Phuong said that Casan is augmented by FPT’s FleziPT AI ecosystem. The results, he says, will be demonstrable in terms of time to market and cost efficiencies, with 60% shaved off development schedules and 30% greater developer productivity. 

FPT is working with giants including Microsoft, Nvidia, SAP and Anthropic to make FleziPT a centrepiece of industrialising AI for enterprises. A July 2026 Forrester Consulting survey, From pilots to reusable platforms: a blueprint for scaling enterprise AI, suggested that only around a quarter of enterprises polled feel advanced in their AI efforts, and FPT believes a ladder approach is needed.

Is Vietnam in the right place at the right time?

With geopolitics fraught and enterprises seeking new sources of innovation as well as lower cost bases, FPT and Vietnam may be in the right place at the right time, just as India once was.

Jon Collins, an analyst at Inter Orbis, said: “I am a great believer in diminishing thresholds and how they either enable new tech platforms – which is how social media suddenly exploded –  or service models. 

“AI is rapidly changing business models around software and service provision, enabling faster-moving organisations anywhere in the world to become players in this ecosystem, where they might previously have been slowed by skills acquisition or other costs of entry. 

“India previously threw its weight into business and technology education to respond to the demand for lower-cost outsourced services, starting with call centres and quickly shifting to more advanced business process outsourcing. With AI including open models, other countries can follow a similar trajectory without requiring such a significant national investment.”

Clients like the speed of work, problem-solving mindset and access to rare skills. 

Ashkan Marandi, head of engineering and product development at Davies Insurance, said: “We partner with FPT because they can provide us with offshore capabilities and speed, and to be able to use the technical experience within the BFSI [banking, financial services and insurance] sector.”

IDC analyst Linus Lai believes FPT’s distinguishing characteristics cover both skills and products: “FPT stands out for combining three things few providers have at once: an owned talent engine through FPT University; platform-led delivery built on reusable IP and a ‘best-shore model’; and a full AI stack that now runs from GPU infrastructure in the AI factory to agentic platforms like IvyHub, where IDC positions them as a Leader in Asia/Pacific.  

“That combination has earned FPT the right to win on execution at scale, which they have done successfully in Japan (their cultural alignment is a big factor in this). The next question is whether FPT can win in more strategic, forward-looking guidance and industry thought leadership. And there is that opportunity to shift toward outcome-based pricing and expand the AI factory globally.”

Of course, FPT and Vietnam have a way to go before they can be compared with India’s remarkable advances on the IT stage. But that formula of combining Western-style ideas, such as Google-like learning campuses, and the hunger of an outsider could be an attractive proposition to many in the West.
